The striped barnacle Amphibalanus amphitrite exhibits a well-documented pattern of larval development that is strongly influenced by water temperature. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the interval from birth to benthic settlement is approximately 8 days , a value that encompasses the six nauplius stages and a brief two-day cyprid phase prior to attachment. Newly hatched nauplii emerge from brood chambers at an exceedingly small size, with an estimated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00000163 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00000163 grams]. This minuscule initial mass reflects the modest egg diameters typical of balanid barnacles and underscores the substantial size increase necessary before metamorphosis can occur, a growth trajectory that spans several orders of magnitude from the earliest larval stage to the fully grown adult.

Following settlement and the metamorphic transition to the juvenile form, Amphibalanus amphitrite individuals undergo a period of rapid somatic growth before reaching key life history milestones. Measurements taken from field-collected specimens indicate that the basal diameter at the time of metamorphosis averages 0.25 centimeters , representing the threshold size at which the cyprid transforms into the first benthic juvenile. This value is critical for understanding early post-settlement survival, as smaller individuals are more vulnerable to physical disturbance and predation on the intertidal substrate where these barnacles typically recruit. The transition from the planktonic cyprid stage to the permanently attached juvenile marks a profound ecological shift, one that determines the spatial distribution of adult populations across available hard surfaces in estuarine and coastal environments.

As growth continues, individuals of Amphibalanus amphitrite eventually attain sexual maturity, which in most Balanus species occurs within a size range of 6 to 9 millimeters in basal diameter. For this species, the basal diameter at puberty has been measured at approximately 0.75 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.75 centimeters], a stage marked by the onset of functional gonad development. This relatively modest size at maturity allows the species to begin reproducing within its first year under favorable thermal conditions, contributing to its success as a dominant fouling organism in warm-temperate and subtropical harbors. The attainment of puberty at this size also implies that individuals allocate a substantial proportion of their assimilated energy toward reproduction rather than continued somatic expansion, a life-history trade-off common among semelparous and iteroparous marine invertebrates.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized in populations maintained at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], revealing a substantial capacity for brood production. Ovigerous females produce between 1,000 and 10,000 eggs per brood [N_R_i = between 1,000 and 10,000 eggs per brood], and individuals are capable of producing up to 24 broods per year [F_R_i = up to 24 broods per year] under these conditions. This high fecundity, coupled with the iteroparous reproductive strategy, enables rapid population expansion when substrate availability is not limiting. The combination of moderate brood size and frequent spawning events yields a daily reproduction rate of approximately 548 eggs per day, a value that places Amphibalanus amphitrite among the more prolific members of the Balanidae when cultured at optimal temperatures.

The ultimate size and longevity of Amphibalanus amphitrite vary considerably across its global range but appear constrained by local thermal regimes. The maximum recorded basal diameter for this species is 1.85 centimeters [Li = 1.85 centimeters], an asymptotic size that the largest adults attain after several years of continuous growth. In populations resident at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the typical life span is approximately 511 days [am = approximately 511 days], reflecting the accelerated metabolic rates and shorter generation times characteristic of warmer-water conspecifics. Ultimate soma wet weight at this maximum size has been estimated at 4.688 grams [Wwi = 4.688 grams], a body mass that supports the energetic demands of repeated reproductive events throughout the adult lifespan. These demographic parameters collectively illustrate the rapid life-history strategy of a warm-water fouling species adapted to unpredictable settlement surfaces and seasonal temperature fluctuations.
